rows.question: Where do rural and city MPs differ on onshore wind?
rows.markdown:
# Rural and city MPs on onshore wind

**Headline:** In the records retrieved, the clearest scepticism comes from rural-seat Conservative backbenchers worried about turbine concentration, as when John Lamont said "many of my constituents in the Scottish borders feel that we now have our fair share of onshore wind" [Source 20]. City-seat MPs more often pressed for onshore wind to expand or for nearby residents to benefit, as when Alan Whitehead urged ministers to "reconsider the remaining planning and funding restrictions on onshore wind so that it really can get going again" [Source 5]. The split is not clean: some rural MPs backed onshore wind through community benefit, and one city MP preferred offshore. The rural sceptics shown are all Conservatives, so the records do not separate seat type from party.

**Rural Conservative backbenchers: sceptical**

David Mundell (Dumfriesshire, Clydesdale and Tweeddale) asked in 2020 for reassurance "that they are not going to be overwhelmed by continuing wind farms" [Source 19].
- John Hayes (South Holland and The Deepings), speaking in 2023, said he "was partly responsible for the moratorium on onshore wind" [Source 14] and that "Offshore wind is infinitely preferable to onshore wind for many reasons" [Source 14].
- Lamont, in 2019, prefaced his concern by saying "I very much support renewable energy" [Source 20].

**Rural MPs: supportive where communities benefit**

Torcuil Crichton (Labour, Na h-Eileanan an Iar) said in 2024 that "community energy is at the heart of much of the wind production in my constituency" [Source 15].
- Tim Yeo (Conservative, South Suffolk; Chair, Energy and Climate Change Committee) suggested in 2014 that host communities might find turbines "less unacceptable than they currently do" [Source 17] if offered an electricity price freeze, adding "but I merely speculate" [Source 17].

**City MPs: mostly supportive, focused on planning and bills**

Alexander Stafford (Conservative, Rother Valley), who said he lives near a wind farm, asked in 2023 that constituents "see the benefits of clean, green wind power reflected in their energy bills" [Source 16].
- Whitehead (Labour shadow minister, Southampton, Test) said in 2023 that "there are precisely zero new schemes in the pipeline in England" [Source 5].
- Geraint Davies (Labour, Swansea West) asked in 2013 whether planning changes would mean "more wind farms in urban areas and fewer in rural areas" [Source 24].

**City dissent: preference for offshore**

James Duddridge (Conservative, Rochford and Southend East) described the offshore wind farms visible from his constituency as "more efficient and cheaper" [Source 18].

**Notes on the evidence**

- The records span 2013 to 2026, and each group rests on two or three speakers.
- Several items are bare questions or statements and do not show a stance. Examples include Alicia Kearns's question on "what steps the Government is taking to make it easier to secure planning permission for new onshore wind turbines" [Source 13], David Chadwick's question on noise limits, and Nick Brown's question on Renewables Obligation Certificates.
- No division records were supplied.

source_text.speaker: Michael Shanks (Labour; MP for Rutherglen, city seat (Greater Glasgow urban area, 1.0m people), Scotland; role on this date: Minister of State (Department for Energy Security and Net Zero)) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 5 June 2026 — UIN 3564 — Department for Energy Security and Net Zero — Wind Power: Government Assistance
source_text.text:
The Government recognises the important role small-scale onshore wind can play in achieving our decarbonisation goals.

The Government supports small-scale onshore wind through the Smart Export Guarantee (SEG), a mechanism that ensures homes or farms with wind turbines receive payments for the renewable electricity they export to the grid.

The Government is also consulting on proposals to introduce a new permitted development right for small-scale, non-domestic wind turbines in England, making it easier for businesses, farms, and public sector organisations to install a single turbine for microgeneration, without needing to submit a full planning application, subject to safeguards.

rows.question: What has been said about NHS waiting lists?
rows.markdown:
**Headline:** In the records retrieved, ministers describe improving waiting-time performance while recognising continued pressures, as when Baroness Merron said ophthalmology waiting times for these services have improved [Source 1]. Labour backbenchers broadly support the Government's aims but press for mental health to be included, with Liz Twist saying "so far mental health services have been excluded from that ambition." [Source 20] Liberal Democrat, Conservative and Reform UK members mainly scrutinise capacity and data, as when Clive Jones described the Government's announcement as "putting the cart before the horse" [Source 15].

**Ministers: defending progress, acknowledging gaps**
Ministers pointed to targets and improvements while recognising delays, as when Preet Kaur Gill, Parliamentary Under-Secretary, wrote on 29 June 2026 that "people are waiting too long to access National Health Service mental health services." [Source 4]
- Stephen Kinnock, Minister of State, said on 22 April 2026 that the Government is committed to returning by March 2029 to the NHS constitutional standard that 92% of patients wait no longer than 18 weeks from referral to consultant-led treatment [Source 6].
- Karin Smyth, Minister of State, wrote on 19 June 2026 that "Validation is a core part of effective waiting list management and we are still behind pre-pandemic levels" [Source 3], citing success in meeting the interim target of 65% referral to treatment performance by the end of March 2026 [Source 3].

**Labour backbenchers: supportive, critical of the previous Government, pressing on mental health**
Labour backbenchers welcomed the Government's plans while blaming the previous Government, as when Satvir Kaur (Southampton Test) said on 23 July 2024: "After 14 years of Conservative mismanagement of our NHS, the waiting list at Southampton general hospital is close to 60,000." [Source 22]
- Liz Twist (Blaydon and Consett) said on 17 June 2026 that "12 times more patients with mental health conditions are waiting longer than 18 months for treatment, compared to those with physical conditions." [Source 20]
- Peter Prinsley (Bury St Edmunds and Stowmarket) asked on 8 September 2026 whether she plans to reinstate the Referral to Treatment (RTT) waiting time data for audiology services [Source 16].

**Liberal Democrats: critical, focused on capacity and local services**
Liberal Democrats were critical of both governments and of capacity, as when Clive Jones (Wokingham) said on 6 January 2025 that "as a result of the last Conservative Government, more patients than ever are waiting for hospital treatments." [Source 15]
- Jones also said "today's announcement regarding the 18-week target pits knee replacements against radiotherapy." [Source 15]
- Baroness Pidgeon, Lords spokesperson, asked about the increase in the ophthalmology waiting list since July 2024 despite reductions in waiting lists across 20 of the NHS's 23 outpatient specialties [Source 7].

**Conservative and Reform UK members: scrutinising data and process**
These members mainly asked questions about how waiting lists are measured, as when Esther McVey (Tatton) asked whether NHS England plans to publish monthly data showing the number of Referral to Treatment pathways removed from waiting lists by reason for removal [Source 12].
- Sarah Pochin (Reform UK, Runcorn and Helsby) asked whether waits between GP referral and being added to an NHS consultant-led elective care waiting list [Source 13] are included in official statistics.
- Edward Argar (Melton and Syston) urged moving more services out of inner-city acute settings and into Melton hospital [Source 17].

*Note:* Many records are written questions without answers, so they show areas of concern rather than stated positions. No division records were supplied.

source_text.speaker: Baroness Merron (Labour; member of the House of Lords; role on this date: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Health and Social Care) — Written answer, Lords written answers — 11 September 2026 — UIN HL2582 — Department of Health and Social Care — Ophthalmic Services: Waiting Lists
source_text.text:
While ophthalmology waiting lists have increased since July 2024, waiting times for these services have improved. The proportion of waits below 18 weeks has increased from 65.7% in July 2024 to 74.1% in May 2026, an 8.4 percentage point improvement.

This Government is committed to returning by March 2029 to the National Health Service constitutional standard that 92% of patients wait no longer than 18 weeks from referral to consultant-led treatment across all specialties, including in ophthalmology services.

We are taking specific steps to improve services like ophthalmology. NHS England accelerator pilots have demonstrated that improved IT connectivity and a single point of access can significantly speed up eye care referrals and support more patients to be managed in the community, in line with the ambitions in the 10-Year Health Plan.

source_text.speaker: Karin Smyth (Labour; MP for Bristol South, city seat (Bristol urban area, 617,000 people), South West; role on this date: Minister of State (Department of Health and Social Care)) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 17 July 2026 — UIN 13650 — Department of Health and Social Care — Health Services: Waiting Lists
source_text.text:
The Department publishes data on Referral to Treatment waiting times. The majority of patients in this data set are considered as having received 'treatment'. A proportion of the removals from the waiting list which appear in this data set as unreported removals, a category which can occur for a variety of data quality and technical reasons, will have been removed for administrative reasons, for example, where a duplicate record was identified. The data is available at the following link:

https://www.england.nhs.uk/statistics/statistical-work-areas/rtt-waiting-times/

source_text.speaker: Karin Smyth (Labour; MP for Bristol South, city seat (Bristol urban area, 617,000 people), South West; role on this date: Minister of State (Department of Health and Social Care)) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 19 June 2026 — UIN 8672 — Department of Health and Social Care — Hospitals: Waiting Lists
source_text.text:
NHS England provided funding to support validation of waiting lists in 2025/26, as part of the Government's plans for a more productive and improved approach to elective care which is better for patients.

Effective waiting list validation means trusts have an accurate understanding of the true size of their waiting list, and helps them to reduce missed or cancelled appointments, ensure clinicians' time is focused on the patients who need it, and reduce overall waiting times.

Validation is a core part of effective waiting list management and we are still behind pre-pandemic levels. Alongside other efforts, including record levels of activity, ensuring clean waiting lists is a key part of our efforts to improve waiting list performance and build on our success in meeting the interim target of 65% referral to treatment performance by the end of March 2026.

source_text.speaker: Preet Kaur Gill (Labour/Co-operative; MP for Birmingham Edgbaston, city seat (West Midlands urban area, 2.4m people), West Midlands; role on this date: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Health and Social Care) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 29 June 2026 — Department of Health and Social Care — Mental Health Services: Waiting Lists
source_text.text:
The Government recognises that people are waiting too long to access National Health Service mental health services. We have already taken significant steps to stabilise and improve NHS mental health services, but there is much more to do. Transforming the system will take time, but we are committed to delivering a new approach through a new mental health strategy for England, which will be published later this year.

Since July 2024, progress has been made in tackling waiting lists for adult community mental health services, alongside continued service expansion. We have recruited 8,500 extra mental health staff, three years ahead of schedule. source_text.speaker: Sharon Hodgson (Labour; MP for Washington and Gateshead South, city seat (Sunderland urban area, 292,000 people), North East; role on this date: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Health and Social Care) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 29 April 2026 — UIN 129107 — Department of Health and Social Care — Cancer: Waiting Lists
source_text.text:
Cancer treatment waiting list data is not published, however, we can provide the latest published 62-day cancer backlog figure, which was 15,102 for the week ending 1 March 2026. The 62-day backlog is the number of patients waiting on the 62-day pathway following an urgent suspected cancer referral. These figures include patients who will not have cancer and are waiting for this to be ruled out as well as those who are waiting for initial treatment following diagnosis of cancer.

For the latest published month of cancer wating time statistics, from February 2026, 3,878 patients were breaching the 31-day treatment standard, and 8,500 patients were breaching the 62-day standard. These patients received a treatment after 31 and 62 days respectively.

source_text.speaker: Stephen Kinnock (Labour; MP for Aberafan Maesteg, city seat (Swansea urban area, 300,000 people), Wales; role on this date: Minister of State (Department of Health and Social Care)) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 22 April 2026 — UIN 127800 — Department of Health and Social Care — Cataracts: Waiting Lists
source_text.text:
As of 12 April 2026, there are 1,124 patients waiting more than 52 weeks for treatment of cataracts within the National Health Service in England.

As set out in the Plan for Change and the Elective Reform Plan, we are committed to returning by March 2029 to the NHS constitutional standard that 92% of patients wait no longer than 18 weeks from referral to consultant-led treatment. As part of this ambition, we are continuing to encourage and support providers to reduce waits for patients who have waited longest for treatment.

The Elective Reform Plan also provides a range of measures to improve the experience of care for patients, including those experiencing long waits. This includes engaging with patients and carers to publish a set of minimum standards that patients can expect to experience in elective care.

source_text.speaker: Baroness Pidgeon (Liberal Democrat; member of the House of Lords; role on this date: Liberal Democrat Lords Spokesperson (Health)) — Written question, Lords written answers — 11 September 2026 — UIN HL2582 — Department of Health and Social Care — Ophthalmic Services: Waiting Lists

source_text.speaker: Stuart Andrew (Conservative; MP for Daventry, rural seat, East Midlands; role on this date: Shadow Secretary of State for Health and Social Care) — Written question, Commons written answers — 1 June 2026 — UIN 1952 — Department of Health and Social Care — Health Services: Waiting Lists
source_text.text: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what steps integrated care boards are required to take when a patient awaiting consultant-led elective treatment has waited longer than 18 weeks from referral to treatment.

rows.question: What arguments were made for and against assisted dying?
rows.markdown:
## Headline

In the records retrieved, supporters argued that assisted dying and palliative care are complementary, as when Peter Prinsley said "Assisted dying is complementary to palliative care; it is not an alternative." [Source 22] Opponents and sceptics raised concerns about gaps in palliative care, pressure on hospices and the future scope of the law, as when Josh Fenton-Glynn said that with "such gaping holes in our health, social care and palliative care system" [Source 21] real choice did not exist. Ministers' written answers stated that "The Government is neutral on the matter of assisted dying" [Source 5].

**Commons supporters (Labour and Liberal Democrat) – supportive, linked to better palliative care**

These MPs rejected an "either/or" framing, as when Pippa Heylings (Liberal Democrat, South Cambridgeshire) said on 11 September 2026 "This is not an either/or. This is not a before/until." [Source 8]
- Layla Moran, Chair of the Health and Social Care Committee, said that "I do not believe that palliative care will improve as fast as we want it to without the pressure of a Bill like this" [Source 1].
- Simon Opher (Labour backbencher, Stroud) said that "in Oregon, 92% of patients who opted for assisted dying were receiving good palliative care. They are different things." [Source 7]

**Commons opponents and sceptics (mainly Conservative, with one Labour and one DUP MP) – hostile or sceptical**

These MPs warned about the Bill's effect on palliative care and its future scope, as when Edward Leigh (Conservative backbencher, Gainsborough) said "I think that in time, it will become an assisted suicide Bill." [Source 14]
- Rebecca Smith (Conservative, South West Devon) said that "all three palliative care doctors who work in Plymouth's Derriford hospital are against assisted dying and are saying that they would leave the profession" [Source 6].
- Jim Shannon (DUP, Strangford) said on 16 May 2025 that "the Bill leaves hospices with little choice but to comply" [Source 24].

**House of Lords – divided**

Peers expressed opposing views. Baroness Keeley (Labour) said "I oppose assisted suicide in principle and I oppose this Bill" [Source 9], whereas Lord Falconer of Thoroton (Labour) said "Assisted dying is about giving somebody a good death. Palliative care is about exactly the same thing." [Source 17]
- Baroness O'Loan (Crossbench) cited research saying that "There are no valid tools, tests, or clinical examinations that can reliably and safely identify that a person is expected to die within six months" [Source 18].
- Lord Kamall, Shadow Health Minister, described himself as "one of those who are still balancing the arguments on the overall Bill" [Source 10].

**Ministers – neutral**

In written answers, ministers left the decision to Parliament. For example, Baroness Merron said that "it is rightly a matter for Parliament to decide if the safeguards in the bill are sufficient" [Source 4].
- Baroness Merron also said that "Irrespective of whether the law changes on assisted dying, we must continue to work towards creating a society where every person who needs it receives high-quality, compassionate palliative care" [Source 2].

*Note: The records retrieved focus heavily on the relationship between assisted dying and palliative care. No division (vote) records were supplied.*

source_text.speaker: Baroness Merron (Labour; member of the House of Lords; role on this date: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Health and Social Care) — Written answer, Lords written answers — 4 December 2025 — UIN HL11759 — Department of Health and Social Care — Euthanasia: Hospices and Palliative Care
source_text.text:
The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill is, first and foremost, a matter for Parliament. This is a Private Member’s Bill, and we cannot pre‑suppose the outcome of the legislative process.

Irrespective of whether the law changes on assisted dying, we must continue to work towards creating a society where every person who needs it receives high-quality, compassionate palliative care and end of life care.

The Government is developing a Palliative Care and End of Life Care Modern Service Framework for England. I refer the noble Lord to the Written Ministerial Statement HLWS1086, which I gave to the House on 24 November 2025.

source_text.text: I refer the Hon. Member to the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill: impact assessment, which considers the resourcing implications of an assisted dying service on palliative and end of life care services.

source_text.speaker: Baroness Merron (Labour; member of the House of Lords; role on this date: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Health and Social Care) — Written answer, Lords written answers — 2 February 2026 — UIN HL12508 — Department of Health and Social Care — Euthanasia
source_text.text:
The purpose of the impact assessment was to appraise the assisted dying service as described in the bill at the end of committee stage. Judicial approval is not one of the steps an applicant must follow to access the assisted dying service. Therefore, no assessment was made regarding the effectiveness of judicial approval as a safeguard.

The Government remains neutral on the policy choices in the bill, and it is rightly a matter for Parliament to decide if the safeguards in the bill are sufficient.

source_text.speaker: Stephen Kinnock (Labour; MP for Aberafan Maesteg, city seat (Swansea urban area, 300,000 people), Wales; role on this date: Minister of State (Department of Health and Social Care)) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 19 June 2025 — UIN 58210 — Department of Health and Social Care — Terminal Illnesses: Suicide
source_text.text:
The Government is neutral on the matter of assisted dying and the passage of the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill.

The Government remains committed to tackling suicide as one the biggest killers in this country and preventing lives being lost.

The suicide prevention strategy identifies priority areas for action to reduce suicide and we will continue to explore opportunities to go further.

source_text.text: I thank the hon. Lady for being so generous with her time. Is she aware of the sheer number of palliative care consultants who are not prepared to take part in assisted dying, and the impact that that will have on the palliative care system? In my constituency, all three palliative care doctors who work in Plymouth’s Derriford hospital are against assisted dying and are saying that they would leave the profession. How can we offer palliative care at the same time as assisted dying?

source_text.text:
No, I will carry on if that is okay.

It is a great thing to offer end-of-life care and palliative care. In 2010, the UK system for palliative care was at the level of the best in the world, yet still people went to Dignitas. Still, 600 people who were suffering from terminal diagnosis killed themselves. Indeed, in Oregon, 92% of patients who opted for assisted dying were receiving good palliative care. They are different things.

source_text.text:

Crucially, it does not even require that those requesting assisted suicide are offered a palliative care assessment first, yet specialists tell us that palliative care can help people who wish to die to rediscover reasons to live. rows.question: What have Labour MPs said about university tuition fees?
rows.markdown:
**Headline:** In the records retrieved, Labour ministers in 2025–26 defended raising tuition fees in line with inflation, describing it as "the difficult decision to increase tuition fees by forecast inflation" [Source 4]. Labour backbenchers in 2026 were divided. One welcomed the increase, while others criticised the fees-and-loans system, and one called to "abolish tuition fees" [Source 10]. In 2021, while Labour was in opposition, two frontbenchers argued for replacing the fee regime, including Matt Western, who said he was "committed to abolishing the fee regime in its current guise" [Source 17].

**Ministers (2025–26) – supportive of inflation-linked rises**

Ministers presented fee increases as necessary for the sector's stability. Georgia Gould, Minister of State, told the House on 18 March 2026 that the increase balanced "the need to give the sector stability with fairness to students and taxpayers" [Source 4].
- Gould said "this Government will link future fees increases to university quality" [Source 4]. She attributed providers' difficulties partly to "a legacy of seven years of frozen tuition fees" [Source 5].
- In a written answer on 11 March 2026, Josh MacAlister said the Government would "increase tuition fee caps for all higher education providers in line with forecast inflation of 2.71% in 2026/27 and 2.68% in 2027/28 and then legislate when parliamentary time allows to increase tuition fee caps automatically for future years" [Source 2].

**Backbenchers (2026) – divided, mostly critical**

Most backbench speakers criticised the current system. Tim Roca (Macclesfield, town seat) said on 25 February 2026 that "England now has the most expensive public university system in the world" [Source 7]. One dissenting voice took a different view: Bayo Alaba (Southend East and Rochford) said on 12 January 2026, "I welcome the Government's actions to support students and universities financially, including through an inflation-based increase to both maintenance loans and tuition fees." [Source 11]
- Rebecca Long-Bailey (Salford, city seat) said "the marketisation of higher education has failed" [Source 10]. She called for replacing tuition fees "with a sustainable, publicly funded model for higher education and university research" [Source 10].
- Mark Sewards (Leeds South West and Morley) said plan 2 loans and "the trebling of tuition fees to £9,000 created a system where those who had to rely on it were essentially paying a graduate tax in all but name" [Source 9].

**Opposition frontbench (2021) – favoured replacing fees**

Speaking in opposition, Labour frontbenchers argued for ending the fee model. Rachael Maskell, Shadow Minister, said on 25 October 2021 that "tuition fees represent a broken system that creates barriers" [Source 23].
- Matt Western, Shadow Minister (Education), said "reducing the maximum rate of student fees merely tinkers with the fees' structure without offering root-and-branch reform" [Source 19].
- Maskell said she did "not support a graduate tax as an alternative to university tuition fees" [Source 23]. She favoured "paying for it through our general taxation system" [Source 23].

**Note on the records:** Several 2026 contributions, including Meg Hillier's Treasury Committee statement, focused mainly on loan repayment terms rather than fee levels. Written questions on fees, such as Andrew Cooper's on "the potential impact of the upcoming rise in undergraduate tuition fees on the take up of university courses by students from deprived backgrounds" [Source 16], were supplied without answers. No division records were supplied.

source_text.speaker: Josh MacAlister (Labour; MP for Whitehaven and Workington, town seat (urban area of 27,000), North West; role on this date: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 5 October 2026 — UIN 23747 — Department for Education — Students: Debts
source_text.text:
Tuition fee loans ensure that higher education (HE) is effectively free at the point of entry for eligible students, removing the need for upfront payment of tuition fees.

Approved (fee cap) HE providers in England are subject to maximum fee limits set in regulations.

Eligible students studying undergraduate courses at these providers in England can apply for tuition fee loans to cover the full regulated tuition fees charged.

Tuition fee loans are paid directly to providers by the Student Loans Company. This removes the need for eligible students to pay regulated tuition fees upfront.

source_text.speaker: Josh MacAlister (Labour; MP for Whitehaven and Workington, town seat (urban area of 27,000), North West; role on this date: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 11 March 2026 — UIN 117320 — Department for Education — Higher Education: Finance
source_text.text:
Around £10.8 billion in tuition fee loans administered by the Student Loans Company were paid directly to higher education providers in the 2024/25 financial year.

To provide long-term funding certainty for the sector, so that it can focus on reform, we will increase tuition fee caps for all higher education providers in line with forecast inflation of 2.71% in 2026/27 and 2.68% in 2027/28 and then legislate when parliamentary time allows to increase tuition fee caps automatically for future years.

We expect the sector to demonstrate that, in return for the increased investment that we are asking students to make, they deliver the best outcomes for those students and the country.

source_text.speaker: Janet Daby (Labour; MP for Lewisham East, city seat (Greater London urban area, 8.1m people), London; role on this date: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 29 April 2025 — UIN 46425 — Department for Education — Universities: Finance
source_text.text:

The graduate visa enables international students who have successfully completed an eligible qualification to stay in the UK for two years, or three years for doctoral students.

Data from the Higher Education Statistics Agency shows that international students contributed £12.1 billion in tuition fees to UK HE providers in the 2022/23 academic year.

This government has made clear its approach to international students. We welcome international students who enrich our university campuses, forge lifelong friendships with our domestic students and become global ambassadors for the UK.

source_text.text:
My hon. Friend makes an important contribution to this debate.

The Government have taken the tough, immediate action that is required, including by making the difficult decision to increase tuition fees by forecast inflation, balancing the need to give the sector stability with fairness to students and taxpayers. We are also asking more of the sector: we expect higher education providers to demonstrate that they deliver the very best outcomes, both for those students and for the country, in return for the increased investment we are asking students to make. To achieve this, this Government will link future fees increases to university quality, as I have said. This will protect taxpayers’ investment in higher education and incentivise high-quality provision for students without taking away opportunities.

rows.question: What have northern MPs said about rail services?
rows.markdown:
**Headline:** In the records retrieved, northern MPs fall into two main positions: backbench and opposition MPs criticise the reliability of Northern and TransPennine Express, as when Lisa Smart described them as "two of the most unreliable train operating companies" [Source 7], while several backbenchers support Northern Powerhouse Rail, as when Alex Sobel said he "warmly welcome[d] the news today that we will finally get Northern Powerhouse Rail" [Source 8]. Government ministers' written answers describe ongoing management work, for example that "Every effort is taken to ensure the planned formation of trains is provided." [Source 3]

**Ministers (2024–2026): measured, describing ongoing work**
Ministers set out existing arrangements and plans, as when Simon Lightwood stated that "The Government is actively considering improvements between Liverpool and Manchester" [Source 4].
- Keir Mather (27 November 2025) said Rail North Partnership works with operators "to deliver the reliable services passengers in the North East want and deserve, taking account of operational and financial constraints" [Source 2].
- Lightwood (20 May 2025) said "we are maintaining momentum on Northern Powerhouse Rail by progressing planning and design works to support future delivery" [Source 4].

**Opposition frontbench and backbenchers: critical of reliability**
These MPs criticised performance across several years, as when Mary Creagh (Wakefield, 2019) said "2018 was an abysmal year for rail travel" [Source 24].
- Louise Haigh, then Shadow Transport Secretary (11 May 2023), said "The comprehensive failure of TransPennine Express is not a bug in the system; it is a feature of it." [Source 13]
- Grahame Morris (Easington, town seat, 2025) said his constituents had "just one overcrowded two-carriage train an hour, which is often cancelled or delayed" [Source 10], while welcoming investment in new trains.

**Backbenchers: supportive of Northern Powerhouse Rail, with local concerns**
Support spanned city, town and rural seats, but town and rural MPs stressed local inclusion, as when Sarah Russell (Congleton, town seat) said NPR "will be great for economic growth across the north" [Source 11] but travel is currently "usually terrible" [Source 11].
- Paul Howell (Sedgefield, rural seat, 2022) said "it is not Manchester Powerhouse Rail or Leeds Powerhouse Rail? It is Northern Powerhouse Rail and that includes the north-east." [Source 23]
- Andrew Jones (Conservative, Harrogate and Knaresborough, 2021) said "I am a big supporter of HS2 and Northern Powerhouse Rail" [Source 21].
- Others asked about delivery, such as Elsie Blundell on "the deliverability of the Northern Powerhouse Rail project" [Source 20] and Sarah Hall on "when Northern Powerhouse Rail will be complete" [Source 19].

**Rail freight and reform: one Liberal Democrat voice**
In the records retrieved, one MP raised freight capacity under reform: Lisa Smart (3 June 2026) warned that "Without explicit protections for freight, there is a real risk that freight corridors will be eroded over time." [Source 6]

*Note: no division records were supplied, and the records span 2015–2026, so stances are not directly comparable across periods.*

rows.question: What has been said about the two-child benefit cap since the 2024 election?
rows.markdown:
**Briefing: the two-child limit since July 2024**

In the records retrieved, ministers and Labour members supported removing the two-child limit, as when Baroness Sherlock said it is the fastest and most cost-effective way to do so [Source 4]. Conservatives defended it, with Joy Morrissey saying we need to keep the two-child benefit cap [Source 23]. Members of smaller parties and some Labour backbenchers welcomed removal but argued that the overall benefit cap would limit its effect, as Ann Davies (Plaid Cymru) did when she said more than one in five households affected by the two-child limit will not benefit because of the cap on benefits [Source 13].

**Ministers: supportive, with the benefit cap kept**

Ministers defended removal while keeping the overall cap, as when Baroness Sherlock (DWP Minister, 10 December 2025) said "The benefit cap is still in place, encouraging parents to take responsibility and work towards financial independence." [Source 4]
- Stephen Timms (DWP Minister, written answer, 30 March 2026) said the two child‑ limit in Child Tax Credit and Universal Credit will be removed from 6th April 2026. [Source 2]
- On 27 April 2026, Timms said the estimate of 450,000 fewer children in poverty takes full account of the benefit cap, which is modelled in both the baseline and policy projections. [Source 1]

**Labour backbenchers and committee chairs: strongly supportive, some with benefit cap concerns**

Labour backbenchers were strongly supportive, as when Fleur Anderson (Putney, London city seat, 3 February 2026) said "I am glad that we are dismantling this cruel and unfair policy today" [Source 21].
- Helen Hayes (Chair, Education Committee) said the Bill will be transformative for families. I am proud to vote for it today. [Source 11]
- Rachael Maskell (York Central, town seat, 23 February 2026) welcomed removal but cited the Joseph Rowntree Foundation finding that 50,000 children—the poorest of our children—will get no benefit whatsoever because of the benefit cap [Source 24]. In the Lords, Lord Sikka raised a similar concern about the overall limit (I am concerned that thousands of children will not receive any improvement from this Bill [Source 19]).

**Other opposition parties and independents: supportive of removal, critical of the benefit cap**

These members backed removal while pressing on the overall cap, as when Ann Davies (Caerfyrddin, rural seat) urged the Secretary of State to legislate to scrap the benefit cap alongside the two-child limit [Source 22].
- Baroness Bennett of Manor Castle (Green) called the limit a cruel policy [Source 15] but described the Bill as a missed opportunity, as it fails to act on the household benefit cap. [Source 15]
- Jeremy Corbyn (Independent, Islington North) said leaving the cap in place will lead to a massive anomaly with other children driven into poverty [Source 17].

**Conservatives: opposed to removal**

Conservatives framed the limit as a matter of fairness to taxpayers, as when Viscount Younger of Leckie (Shadow Minister, 10 December 2025) said it was to make the benefits system fairer to taxpayers who support themselves and their families solely through work [Source 9].
- Lord Farmer asked whether lifting the two-child limit will incentivise more births in benefit-dependent households [Source 18].
- Joy Morrissey (Beaconsfield, town seat) described it as an issue of fairness for the taxpayer [Source 23].

*Notes: No division records were supplied, so voting figures cannot be reported. The only Liberal Democrat material in the records retrieved is a written question from Freddie Van Mierlo and a reference by Janet Daby to that party's support.*

source_text.speaker: Stephen Timms (Labour; MP for East Ham, city seat (Greater London urban area, 8.1m people), London; role on this date: Minister for Equalities (Department for Education); The Minister of State, Department for Work and Pensions) — Written answer, Commons written answers — 27 April 2026 — UIN 128434 — Department for Work and Pensions — Universal Credit: Children
source_text.text:
The Department for Work and Pensions’ Policy Simulation Model (PSM) was used to model the impact of the removal of the two-child limit on Universal Credit. The PSM uses household characteristics, caseload forecasts and benefit rules to estimate policy impacts for each year, currently up to and including FYE 2031.

It is estimated that there will be 450,000 fewer children in relative poverty after housing costs in the final year of parliament (FYE 2030) as a result of the removal of the two-child limit within Universal Credit, compared to baseline projections. This estimate takes full account of the benefit cap, which is modelled in both the baseline and policy projections.

source_text.text:
The Government has announced that the two child‑ limit in Child Tax Credit and Universal Credit will be removed from 6th April 2026.

For Universal Credit, the Department is contacting customers who are expected to benefit from the removal of the two child limit directly, ensuring that families are aware of the additional support they will be entitled to. Eligible customers will automatically receive the increased child element from April 2026, provided the number of children in their household is correctly recorded on their Universal Credit claim.

The Universal Credit service will be updated to reflect the policy change, and agents will receive updated guidance and communications to support them in responding to claimant enquiries. Customers can also receive additional support through Jobcentres, by telephoning the Universal Credit helpline, or via their online Universal Credit account

source_text.text: My Lords, children should not grow up in poverty. It is bad for them, bad for their aspirations and, ultimately, bad for the country. Parents who are foreign nationals can access universal credit only with a valid immigration status of a kind that gives them the right to access public funds.

source_text.speaker: Viscount Younger of Leckie (Conservative; member of the House of Lords; role on this date: Shadow Minister (Work and Pensions)) — House of Lords — 10 December 2025 — col. 232 — Universal Credit: Two-child Limit - Question
source_text.text:
My Lords, can I bring the House back to the original intention behind the two-child limit? It was to make the benefits system fairer to taxpayers who support themselves and their families solely through work. It encouraged parents on benefit to make the same financial choices about family size as those not on benefits. With the Government’s poverty argument in mind, the IFS has said that reversing the two-child limit is “not a silver bullet”. It said that the benefit cap will

“wipe out the gains for some children in the … poorest families”,

as 70,000 more households are affected by the cap. Surely supporting parents into work and into quality jobs is much more important for reducing child poverty. Finally, the IFS says that raising the employment rate to 80% from the current 75% would lift up to 350,000 children out of poverty.

rows.question: How have ministers defended energy price policy?
rows.markdown:
**Headline:** In the records retrieved, ministers of both parties defended energy price policy partly by saying the level of the cap is for Ofgem: Greg Hands in 2022 said "The setting of the level of the Energy Price Cap is a matter for Ofgem" [Source 20], and Baroness Curran in 2026 said "the Government does not speculate on such matters" [Source 1]. Conservative ministers in 2022–24 defended direct subsidy through the Energy Price Guarantee. Labour ministers from 2024 presented clean power as the long-term answer and, in 2026, cited specific reductions to bills.

**Conservative ministers (2022–24): defending the Energy Price Guarantee**

These ministers defended the guarantee's cost and design, as when Graham Stuart, Minister for Climate, said on 18 November 2022 that "The Government does not pay any premium to energy suppliers." [Source 16]
- Jacob Rees-Mogg, Business Secretary, told the House on 17 October 2022 that "the Prime Minister announced an unprecedented package of assistance" [Source 21].
- Andrew Bowie, Under-Secretary, said on 29 June 2023 that "the tariff cap was always intended to be a temporary measure" [Source 18].

**Labour ministers (2024–25): clean power as the long-term remedy**

Labour ministers attributed price rises to wholesale fossil fuel markets, as when Miatta Fahnbulleh, Under-Secretary, said on 14 October 2024 that "the only way to protect consumers permanently is to speed up the transition towards homegrown clean energy" [Source 7].
- Michael Shanks, Minister of State, described elevated wholesale gas costs on 8 September 2025 as "the fossil fuel penalty being paid by families, businesses and our economy" [Source 5].
- Lord Hunt of Kings Heath said on 26 March 2025 that "the Government are reviewing Ofgem's role to ensure that it is a strong consumer champion" [Source 17].

**Labour ministers (2026): pointing to bill reductions**

In 2026 the defence centred on specific measures, as when Baroness Curran said on 5 August 2026 that "Tackling affordability is this Government's number one priority" [Source 1], citing the removal of VAT from electricity bills and £150 of costs taken off energy bills.
- Torsten Bell, answering for the Treasury on 8 September 2026, said the VAT removal "will take around £45 off the annual Ofgem price cap" [Source 11] and that the Budget action was "reducing inflation by around 0.2 percentage points in 2026/27" [Source 11].
- Polly Billington, Under-Secretary, said the same day that "The latest increase in energy bills is driven by increased wholesale energy costs, particularly gas, due to the ongoing situation in the Middle East." [Source 2]

*Note: The records are mostly written answers from ministers. They contain no opposition or backbench responses and no division records.*

source_text.text:

We also acted at last year’s Budget by taking on average £150 of costs off energy bills, with those decisions now factored into bills for the years to come.

The Government continues to monitor energy prices closely and recognises the impact that changes in bills can have on households.

The latest increase in energy bills is driven by increased wholesale energy costs, particularly gas, due to the ongoing situation in the Middle East. In addition, this Government took an average £150 of costs off bills at the Autumn budget, w

source_text.text:

The independent industry regulator Ofgem sets different price cap limits across regions to reflect differences in network costs for maintaining infrastructure.

rows.question: What has Hilary Benn said about Northern Ireland?
rows.markdown:
# Hilary Benn on Northern Ireland: briefing

**Headline:** The records retrieved contain two contributions from Hilary Benn, both made as Secretary of State for Northern Ireland in the House of Commons on 25 March 2026. In them he spoke positively about the Good Friday agreement, as when he said that "nearly 30 years ago" it "brought an end to the troubles and enabled Northern Ireland to establish a power-sharing Government" [Source 2]. He also defended the Windsor framework as a response to post-Brexit border issues, saying "that is what the Windsor framework seeks to do" [Source 1].

*Note: all evidence comes from one speaker on one date. The sections below group his remarks by theme rather than by groups of speakers, and no wider pattern should be inferred.*

**Good Friday agreement: supportive and forward-looking**

Benn described the agreement as the basis of Northern Ireland's progress, saying that "In the years since, Northern Ireland has been transformed, and I look forward to working with everyone to make further progress." [Source 2]
- He noted the coming anniversary: "On 10 April we will celebrate the anniversary of the Good Friday agreement" [Source 2].
- Replying to an unnamed member, he said: "I do not accept the hon. and learned Gentleman's argument in relation to the Good Friday agreement." [Source 1] The records do not include that member's argument.

**Windsor framework and Brexit: defending the framework, critical of leave advocates**

Benn presented the framework as addressing problems he attributed to those who campaigned to leave the EU. He said that "those who advocated to leave the European Union did not think about the consequences for having two entities and one open border and how we could ensure that goods crossing the border would meet the rules of the respective entity" [Source 1].

**Relations with the EU: supportive of a new agreement**

Benn pointed to further negotiations with the EU and to cross-party backing for them in Northern Ireland. He told the House that "The Government are negotiating a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement with the EU, which has been widely welcomed by all parties across Northern Ireland." [Source 1]

**What the records do not cover**

The supplied records contain nothing from Benn on these subjects:
- the Stormont brake
- Northern Ireland's budget or public services
- legacy issues
- reform of the power-sharing institutions

They contain no statements by him before 25 March 2026 and no division (vote) records. Other contributions in the supplied material, such as those from Peter Kyle, Lord Bew and Jim Allister, are by different speakers and are not covered here.

## Childcare policy: women and men in Parliament

**Headline:** The records retrieved show no clear difference between women and men on childcare policy. Ministers of both genders described the funded-hours expansion in positive terms, as when Claire Coutinho said it represents the single biggest investment in childcare in England [Source 17] and David Johnston said "We are removing one of the biggest barriers for working parents" [Source 10]. The only probing contributions come from one man, a select committee chair, and one woman, an opposition spokesperson.

**Women: supportive (ministers), with one questioning voice**

Women ministers described the policy positively, as when Andrea Jenkyns (Parliamentary Under-Secretary, Education) said on 26 October 2022: "We are committed to improving the cost, choice, and availability of childcare." [Source 24]
- Olivia Bailey (Labour minister), 20 April 2026: "In 2026/27, we are expecting to provide over £9.5 billion for the early years entitlements" [Source 1].
- Munira Wilson (Liberal Democrat spokesperson), 7 April 2025, asked how many eligible two-year-olds were unable to take up those hours due to shortage of nursery places [Source 19]. No answer to her question is included in the records.

**Men: supportive (ministers), with one critical backbench voice**

Men ministers also presented the expansion positively, as when Paul Waugh (Labour minister) said on 5 August 2026 that a survey found that the expansion of 30 hours of funded childcare significantly reduced costs for eligible working parents in England [Source 2].
- Robin Walker (Conservative, Chair of the Education Committee), 16 October 2023, said the sector had faced a crisis of both affordability and availability [Source 12]. He also said: "My biggest disappointment with the announcements made at the Budget is that the tax-free childcare system was not touched" [Source 12].
- Walker also argued that it was counterproductive to disincentivise parents from pursuing higher qualifications by making 30 hours of childcare available only to working families on a particular income [Source 12].

**Where the two groups said similar things**

On the Tax-Free Childcare cap, women and men Treasury ministers gave closely matching answers. John Glen and Darren Jones both said the £2,000 top-up strikes the right balance between helping parents with their childcare costs [Source 5][Source 15] and managing the public finances. Laura Trott said the Government recognises the importance of supporting parents with the costs of childcare and continues to support families with a range of other childcare offers [Source 14]. Women and men education ministers also described the 30-hours offer in similar terms. Coutinho said it aims to support working families with the cost of childcare, and to support parents back into work [Source 13], and Johnston said the entitlement aims to help with the costs of childcare so that parents can take up paid work if they want to or work additional hours [Source 11].

*Note on the evidence:* Most records are ministerial written answers setting out government policy. Only two contributions come from members who were not ministers: one debate speech and two written questions. No division (vote) records were supplied. The records therefore cannot support any general conclusion about how women and men in Parliament differ on childcare.

rows.question: Why are Tory MPs so heartless about benefit claimants?
rows.markdown:
# Conservative MPs on benefit claimants: sanctions, overpayments and safeguards

The records cannot show whether any MP is "heartless". They show what was said, and this briefing reports that.

In the records retrieved, Conservative ministers defended sanctions and the recovery of overpayments as a balance between duty to the taxpayer and support for claimants. David Rutley said "We need to balance our duty to the taxpayer with the need to deal with customers sensitively and appropriately." [Source 7] Several ministerial answers stated that no assessment had been made, or was planned, of particular effects on claimants, as when Guy Opperman said "There are currently no plans to undertake further research on sanctions." [Source 3] The backbench records are written questions seeking data, with no stated stance. One example is Peter Bedford's request for statistics on the number of claimants who lose their (a) Personal Independence Payment and b) Universal Credit health entitlement [Source 17].

**Ministers on sanctions – supportive, with stated safeguards**

Ministers presented sanctions as part of conditionality, as when Steve Barclay, Chief Secretary to the Treasury, said on 1 March 2021 that "Sanctions are a core element of the conditionality approach to helping people back into work" [Source 23].

- Alok Sharma (DWP Minister of State) said on 10 December 2018 that "Sanctions are only used in a small percentage of cases, and that is when people fail to meet their agreed commitments without good reason." [Source 18]
- Jo Churchill (DWP Minister of State) pointed on 4 December 2023 to "a well-established system of hardship payments" [Source 4] for sanctioned claimants.

**Ministers on overpayments and debt – supportive of recovery**

Ministers defended recovering overpayments, including those caused by official error. On 21 July 2022 David Rutley (Parliamentary Under-Secretary, DWP) told the House that "we do not think it is unreasonable that all overpayments are repayable." [Source 7]

- Rutley said the current deduction limits "strike the right balance between managing the social obligations while supporting claimants with debt." [Source 7]
- Will Quince (Parliamentary Under-Secretary, DWP) noted on 14 July 2021 "two successive reductions in the maximum that may normally be deducted – from 40% of the UC Standard Allowance to 30% and now 25% from April 2021." [Source 13]

**Ministers on assessing impacts – no assessment made or planned**

Several answers stated that impacts had not been assessed. On 30 November 2023 Jo Churchill said that "no assessment has been made of the potential impact of removing a parents' entitlement to benefits on their children." [Source 2]

- Victoria Prentis (DWP Minister of State) said on 29 September 2022 that "The Department has taken the decision not to proceed with this data sharing project" [Source 5]. The project was a University of Glasgow study of the health impacts of sanctions.
- Alok Sharma said on 20 March 2019 that "The Department has not made an assessment of the effect of imposing sanctions on disabled Universal Credit claimants" [Source 12]. He added that the Department committed to evaluating the effectiveness of reforms to welfare conditionality and sanctions [Source 12].

**Backbenchers (2024–25) – questions only, no stance stated**

The backbench records are requests for information, as when Neil O'Brien (Harborough, Oadby and Wigston) asked "how many phone calls to report hospital stays for claimants... there were in each month since January 2010." [Source 19]

- Nick Timothy (West Suffolk) asked how many benefits claimant households received (a) Universal Credit... and (e) legacy benefits in each year since 2010, broken down by local authority. [Source 22]

*The records retrieved do not include Commons debate contributions from Conservative backbenchers, and no division records were supplied.*

source_text.text:
In October this year, the Work and Pensions Select Committee set out recommendations relating to the economic and health effects of sanctions, which the Department is considering and will be responding to in due course.

Sanctions are only used in a small percentage of cases, and that is when people fail to meet their agreed commitments without good reason. Latest data, published 12 November in the Benefit Sanction Statistics, shows that in August 2018, 2.9% of people subject to conditionality on Universal Credit had a deduction taken from their benefit award as a result of a sanction.

When considering whether a sanction is appropriate, a Decision Maker will take all the claimant’s individual circumstances, including any health conditions or disabilities and any evidence of good cause, into account before deciding whether a sanction is warranted.

source_text.text:
In the Welfare Reform Bill we will be introducing a claimant commitment, which will set out the responsibilities of benefit recipients, alongside a clear and robust set of sanctions. Claimants will therefore know what they are expected to do and the consequences of failing to meet those expectations. These changes will be introduced under the current benefit system and will continue to apply under universal credit.

The proposed model of sanctions could lead to longer sanctions for some claimants, particularly claimants who have repeatedly failed to meet their responsibilities. For other claimants-those who fail to meet lower level requirements-sanctions could be shorter depending on how quickly they re-engage.

source_text.text:

Sanctions are a core element of the conditionality approach to helping people back into work, and DWP work coaches will ensure that they are only ever used in a proportionate, reasonable way. In universal credit, jobseeker's allowance and new style employment and support allowance, sanctions are only considered where a claimant has not undertaken a work-related requirement as agreed in their Claimant Commitment without good reason. A personalised, tailored Claimant Commitment is agreed between the work coach and the claimant. They will only set reasonable requirements, based on the claimant’s circumstances and the local/national health guidelines – and no claimant can or will be sanctioned without a Claimant Commitment in place.
